sectionTitle: Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves

specStatements.text: Electromagnetic waves have many practical applications. For example:
• infrared – electrical heaters, cooking food, infrared cameras
• ultraviolet – energy efficient lamps, sun tanning
• X-rays and gamma rays – medical imaging and treatments.
(HT only) Students should be able to give brief explanations why each type of electromagnetic wave is suitable for the practical application.

scopeNotes.statement: Electromagnetic waves have many practical applications. For example:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification introduces the list with 'For example', so the pairings that follow are exemplars, not an exhaustive syllabus of uses. Every item here is built on an application the specification actually names – television and radio; satellite communications and cooking food; electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras; fibre optic communications; energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; medical imaging and treatments. No question requires a student to recall an application the specification does not list, and no question asks for the engineering detail of a device (aerial design, magnetron operation, fibre manufacture) that lies outside this section.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) Students should be able to give brief explanations why each type of electromagnetic wave is suitable for the practical application.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Explanation of suitability is marked HT only, so the two items that demand it (q11, q12) carry tier 'higher'. Foundation-tier items in this section ask only which group of waves is used for a named application and what happens when that radiation is absorbed; they never require a student to justify the choice of wave. The specification also asks for 'brief' explanations, so the higher-tier items are answered in a single reason – transmission through the atmosphere, absorption by a coating – rather than a quantitative treatment.

concepts.term: Practical application of an electromagnetic wave
concepts.definition: A use made of one group of the electromagnetic spectrum. The specification lists radio waves with television and radio; microwaves with satellite communications and cooking food; infrared with electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras; visible light with fibre optic communications; ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; and X-rays and gamma rays with medical imaging and treatments.

Radio waves are the longest-wavelength group of the spectrum and are used to broadcast television and radio programmes. A transmitter converts the signal into radio waves, and an aerial on a house or a receiver picks them up and converts them back.

concepts.term: Microwaves – satellite communications and cooking food
concepts.definition: Microwaves have shorter wavelengths than radio waves. They are used to carry signals up to satellites and back down to earth, and in a microwave oven, where they are absorbed by the food and increase its energy store.

Infrared is emitted by all objects, and by more the hotter they are. It is used in electrical heaters and grills, where it is absorbed by the surface it falls on, and in infrared cameras, which form an image from the infrared an object emits.
Visible light is the narrow band of the spectrum the eye detects. In fibre optic communications, information is sent as very rapid pulses of light that travel along a thin glass fibre.

concepts.term: Ultraviolet – energy efficient lamps and sun tanning
concepts.definition: Ultraviolet has shorter wavelengths than visible light. It is produced inside an energy efficient (fluorescent) lamp and converted to visible light by the coating on the tube, and it is used in sunbeds and sunlight to tan skin, though it can damage skin cells.

concepts.term: X-rays and gamma rays – medical imaging and treatments
concepts.definition: X-rays and gamma rays are the shortest-wavelength groups. They are used to make images of the inside of the body, because bone absorbs them far more than soft tissue does, and in treatment, where a beam is directed at a tumour to destroy its cells.

concepts.term: Absorption and transmission decide the use (HT)
concepts.definition: Whether a wave is suitable for an application depends on what absorbs it and what lets it through. Microwaves suit satellite links because the atmosphere transmits them; infrared suits a grill because food absorbs it; X-rays suit imaging because bone absorbs them and flesh does not.

The layer on the inside of an energy efficient lamp that absorbs the ultraviolet produced in the tube and re-emits the energy as visible light, so the lamp lights the room without releasing ultraviolet into it.

misconceptions.question: Food in a microwave oven is heated from the middle outwards, so the centre is always hottest.
misconceptions.correct: Microwaves are absorbed as they enter the food and transfer energy to it; the energy then spreads through the rest of the food.
misconceptions.misconception: Microwaves travel straight to the centre and cook the food from the inside out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'cooks from the inside out' is repeated so often that students take it literally, and it seems to explain why microwaved food can be hot in the middle and cool at the edges – which is really uneven absorption and uneven spreading of energy.
misconceptions.correction: Microwaves are absorbed mainly in the outer few centimetres of the food, and energy spreads inwards by conduction. A microwave oven is faster than a grill because energy is delivered throughout that outer layer rather than only to the surface, not because heating starts in the centre.

misconceptions.question: Food that has been in a microwave oven is slightly radioactive afterwards.
misconceptions.correct: The food absorbs microwaves and its temperature rises; nothing about the food becomes radioactive.
misconceptions.misconception: 'Radiation' from the oven makes the food radioactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The single word 'radiation' is used for electromagnetic waves and for nuclear radiation, so students transfer everything they know about the second to the first.
misconceptions.correction: Microwaves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Absorbing them raises the energy store of the food, exactly as absorbing infrared from a grill does. Only processes that change the nuclei of atoms can make something radioactive, and microwaves cannot do that.

misconceptions.question: All cooking appliances – grills, toasters, ovens – cook food with microwaves.
misconceptions.correct: Only a microwave oven uses microwaves; a grill or toaster cooks with infrared emitted by its hot elements.
misconceptions.misconception: Any appliance that cooks does so with microwaves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The microwave oven is the cooking application students meet in this topic, so 'microwaves cook food' is generalised to every cooker.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists cooking food under both microwaves and infrared. A glowing element emits infrared, which the surface of the food absorbs; a microwave oven emits microwaves, which penetrate a few centimetres before being absorbed.

misconceptions.question: Signals sent to a communications satellite are carried by radio waves, because radio waves travel the furthest.
misconceptions.correct: Microwaves are used for satellite communications.
misconceptions.misconception: Radio waves are used for every long-distance link, including satellites.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radio waves are introduced as the waves used for broadcasting over long distances, and everyday speech calls any transmitted signal a 'radio signal', so satellites are assumed to use them as well.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio, and microwaves with satellite communications. Microwaves are used because they pass through the atmosphere to the satellite; many radio waves are reflected or absorbed instead.

misconceptions.question: A sunbed tans the skin with infrared, because tanning is caused by the heat you can feel.
misconceptions.correct: Ultraviolet is what tans the skin.
misconceptions.misconception: The warmth felt from the lamp, which is infrared, causes the tan.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sunbathing feels hot, and heat is the sensation students associate with a tan, so the tan is credited to infrared rather than to the radiation that cannot be felt at all.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs sun tanning with ultraviolet. Ultraviolet is absorbed by skin cells and causes them to produce more pigment; it can also damage those cells. Infrared warms the skin but does not tan it.

misconceptions.question: Ultraviolet is the light you see coming out of a lamp.
misconceptions.correct: Ultraviolet cannot be seen by the human eye; it lies just beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet is a kind of visible light, so a glowing lamp is shining ultraviolet at you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name contains 'violet', and ultraviolet is drawn on spectrum diagrams right next to the coloured band, so students place it inside the visible range.
misconceptions.correction: The visible spectrum ends at violet. Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength than any colour the eye can detect, which is why the ultraviolet made inside an energy efficient lamp is invisible and why a sunbed can burn skin that feels nothing unusual.

misconceptions.question: An energy efficient lamp is designed to send ultraviolet out into the room.
misconceptions.correct: The ultraviolet is produced inside the tube and converted into visible light by the coating before it leaves the lamp.
misconceptions.misconception: Because ultraviolet is listed under energy efficient lamps, the lamp must shine ultraviolet into the room.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification pairs ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps, and students read the pairing as 'what comes out' rather than 'what is used inside'.
misconceptions.correction: Ultraviolet is a step in how the lamp works, not its output. The coating on the inside of the tube absorbs ultraviolet and re-emits visible light, so the room is lit by visible light.

misconceptions.question: An infrared camera works by shining a beam on to the scene so that the camera can see it.
misconceptions.correct: An infrared camera detects the infrared that warm objects give out by themselves.
misconceptions.misconception: The camera must light up the scene before it can form an image.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every camera students have used needs light, and a flash is the obvious way to photograph in the dark, so an emitter is assumed rather than a detector.
misconceptions.correction: All objects emit infrared, and warmer objects emit more. An infrared camera forms an image from that emitted radiation, which is why a person shows up in complete darkness and why the image shows the warm and cool parts of an object.

misconceptions.question: Infrared can be seen – it is the red glow you see from a heater or a grill.
misconceptions.correct: Infrared is invisible; the red glow is visible light that the very hot element also emits.
misconceptions.misconception: The red colour of a hot element is the infrared radiation itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'infrared' contains 'red', and the two are emitted together by anything hot enough to glow, so the visible glow is taken as proof that infrared is visible.
misconceptions.correction: A heater that is not glowing at all still emits plenty of infrared, and an infrared camera detects people who give out no visible light. Infrared lies beyond red, at wavelengths the eye cannot detect.

misconceptions.question: Ultraviolet from a sunbed is safe, because the exposure is short and controlled.
misconceptions.correct: Ultraviolet from a sunbed can damage skin cells however it is delivered.
misconceptions.misconception: A controlled indoor dose of ultraviolet carries no risk.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sunbeds are sold as a managed alternative to the sun, and the risk from sunlight is presented as a sunburn risk, so an indoor lamp with a timer feels harmless.
misconceptions.correction: It is the ultraviolet itself that is absorbed by skin cells, and the source makes no difference. The specification lists sun tanning as an application of ultraviolet while treating that radiation as one that can harm skin.

misconceptions.question: On an X-ray photograph, the X-rays get through the bone and are stopped by the flesh around it.
misconceptions.correct: X-rays pass through soft tissue and are absorbed by bone.
misconceptions.misconception: Bone lets X-rays through while flesh absorbs them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The bone appears white and bright on the image, and students read 'bright' as 'the radiation arrived here', which reverses what actually happened.
misconceptions.correction: Bone contains heavier elements and absorbs X-rays strongly, so few reach the detector behind it and a shadow is formed. The image is a shadow picture: pale where absorption was greatest.

misconceptions.question: An X-ray image is formed by X-rays bouncing off the bone back to the film.
misconceptions.correct: The image is a shadow made by X-rays that have passed through the body.
misconceptions.misconception: X-rays reflect from bone the way light reflects from a mirror.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ordinary photography works by reflected light, so students carry the same model across to X-rays without asking whether the radiation goes through the patient.
misconceptions.correction: The detector is on the far side of the patient from the X-ray tube. What reaches it is the radiation that got through, so dense bone leaves a pale shadow while soft tissue leaves a darker region.

misconceptions.question: A patient treated with gamma rays becomes radioactive afterwards.
misconceptions.correct: Being irradiated by gamma rays does not make tissue radioactive.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma treatment leaves the treated tissue giving out radiation of its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Irradiation and contamination are easily confused, and gamma rays come from radioactive sources, so students assume the radioactivity is passed on.
misconceptions.correction: Radioactivity is a property of unstable nuclei. Gamma rays transfer energy to the cells they pass through, damaging them, but they do not turn stable nuclei into unstable ones.

misconceptions.question: Gamma rays are far too dangerous to be used on a person for any reason.
misconceptions.correct: Gamma rays are used in hospitals to treat cancer, with the beam carefully directed and the dose controlled.
misconceptions.misconception: Because gamma rays are hazardous, they can have no medical use.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gamma rays are taught first as the most penetrating and most dangerous radiation, so the hazard is remembered and the controlled application is not.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs X-rays and gamma rays with medical imaging and treatments. The same property that makes gamma rays hazardous – their ability to damage cells – is what allows a directed beam to kill the cells of a tumour.

misconceptions.question: Infrared cannot travel through empty space, because it needs something to carry the heat.
misconceptions.correct: Infrared is an electromagnetic wave and travels through a vacuum, but it is strongly absorbed by the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: Infrared needs a medium, so it cannot cross the vacuum between the earth and a satellite.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Infrared is met as a way of transferring energy from hot objects, alongside conduction and convection, which do need a medium.
misconceptions.correction: Infrared from the Sun crosses 150 million kilometres of vacuum to reach us. The reason microwaves rather than infrared are used for satellite links is that the atmosphere transmits microwaves while it absorbs much of the infrared.

misconceptions.question: A fibre optic cable carries the signal as radio waves or microwaves, because that is what cables and links carry.
misconceptions.correct: A fibre optic cable carries the signal as pulses of visible light.
misconceptions.misconception: Any communication cable or fast link must be carrying radio waves or microwaves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students group all communications together and reach for the waves already labelled 'communication waves', without noticing that the specification lists a separate application for visible light.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs visible light with fibre optic communications. The signal is a rapid train of light pulses travelling along a thin glass fibre, which is why the fibre is transparent rather than metal.

misconceptions.question: Any invisible radiation that is used to send or detect something can be called radio waves.
misconceptions.correct: Each group of the spectrum has its own applications; 'radio waves' names one group only.
misconceptions.misconception: Radio waves are the general name for invisible radiation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radio waves are the first group met, and everyday language uses 'radio' loosely for any wireless signal, so the term expands to cover the whole invisible spectrum.
misconceptions.correction: The spectrum is divided into named groups by wavelength, and the specification gives each its own applications: radio waves for television and radio, microwaves for satellite links and microwave ovens, X-rays and gamma rays for medical imaging.

misconceptions.question: Microwaves travel faster than infrared, which is why microwaves are used to reach satellites.
misconceptions.correct: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum.
misconceptions.misconception: Different groups of the spectrum travel at different speeds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Higher frequency is read as 'more energetic', and 'more energetic' slides into 'faster', especially when the spectrum is drawn as a sequence from weak to strong.
misconceptions.correction: The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous range of waves that all transfer energy at the same speed through a vacuum. Microwaves are chosen for satellite links because the atmosphere lets them through, not because they arrive sooner.

misconceptions.question: A bone shows up on an X-ray because it gives out light of its own when the X-rays hit it.
misconceptions.correct: The bone absorbs X-rays and casts a shadow on the detector.
misconceptions.misconception: The bone is made to glow, and the image records that glow.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The finished image looks like a photograph of something bright, so students invent a source inside the body rather than picturing a shadow.
misconceptions.correction: No radiation is emitted by the bone. X-rays from the tube pass through the patient; bone absorbs most of them, so fewer arrive behind it and that region of the image stays pale.

misconceptions.question: Gamma rays are only ever used to take pictures inside the body.
misconceptions.correct: X-rays and gamma rays are used both for medical imaging and for treatments.
misconceptions.misconception: Imaging is the only medical use of these waves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Imaging is the use students meet first and can picture, and the word 'ray' is tied to X-ray photographs, so treatment is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names both uses: medical imaging and treatments. In treatment a beam of gamma rays is directed at a tumour so that the cells absorbing it are destroyed.

misconceptions.question: If there is a clear line of sight to something, visible light is used to send the signal.
misconceptions.correct: Satellite links use microwaves, even though there is a clear path to the satellite.
misconceptions.misconception: A straight, unobstructed path means the signal must be carried by light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Light is the wave students know travels in straight lines, so line of sight is taken as evidence that light is being used.
misconceptions.correction: All electromagnetic waves travel in straight lines through a uniform medium. The wave chosen for a link depends on what the atmosphere transmits and what the equipment can send and detect, which is why satellite communications use microwaves and fibre optics use visible light.

mcqs.stem: The specification lists a practical application for each group of electromagnetic waves. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Satellite communication uses radio waves
options.rationale: Radio is associated with long-distance broadcasting, so a student extends it to satellites; the specification pairs satellite communications with microwaves.

options.text: Sun tanning lamps mainly give out infrared
options.rationale: Tanning is linked with the warmth felt in sunlight, so infrared is chosen; the specification pairs sun tanning with ultraviolet.

options.text: Fibre optic communications use visible light
options.rationale: The specification pairs visible light with fibre optic communications: the signal travels along the glass fibre as rapid pulses of light.

options.text: A toaster cooks bread using microwaves
options.rationale: A student who ties all cooking to the microwave oven picks this; a toaster cooks with infrared from its glowing elements.

mcqs.stem: Which use does the specification give for radio waves?

options.text: Broadcasting television and radio programmes
options.rationale: The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio.

options.text: Sending signals to and from satellites in orbit
options.rationale: This is the microwave application; calling any transmitted signal a 'radio signal' makes a student claim satellites for radio waves.

options.text: Carrying signals along fibre optic cables
options.rationale: A cable is assumed to carry a radio or electrical signal; a fibre optic cable carries pulses of visible light.

options.text: Taking images of bones inside the body
options.rationale: Any invisible penetrating radiation is labelled 'radio waves'; medical imaging belongs to X-rays and gamma rays.

mcqs.stem: A signal is sent from a ground station up to a satellite in orbit and then back down to a second ground station. Which waves carry the signal?

options.text: Radio waves, which are used for broadcasting today
options.rationale: Radio waves are the first communication waves met, so they are applied to satellite links as well.

options.text: Microwaves, which pass through the atmosphere
options.rationale: The specification pairs microwaves with satellite communications; the atmosphere transmits them, so they reach the satellite and return.

options.text: Infrared, which is given out by all hot objects
options.rationale: Infrared is tied to energy transfer through space from anything hot, so it is offered for the link to the satellite.

options.text: Visible light, which goes in straight lines
options.rationale: A clear line of sight to the satellite suggests light; visible light is used for fibre optics, not satellite links.

mcqs.stem: How does a microwave oven cook food?

options.text: Microwaves heat the middle of the food first
options.rationale: 'Cooks from the inside out' is taken literally, so the centre is assumed to be heated before the outside.

options.text: Microwaves make the food slightly radioactive
options.rationale: 'Radiation' is read as nuclear radiation, so the food is thought to become radioactive.

options.text: A glowing element inside gives out infrared
options.rationale: A conventional oven or grill is pictured instead; a microwave oven has no glowing element doing the cooking.

options.text: The food absorbs microwaves and heats up
options.rationale: Microwaves are absorbed by the food, and the energy transferred raises its temperature.

mcqs.stem: An electric grill glows red and cooks the food placed underneath it. Which radiation transfers energy to the food?

options.text: Microwaves, because all cookers use microwaves
options.rationale: Every cooking appliance is assumed to work like a microwave oven.

options.text: Infrared, which is absorbed by the food surface
options.rationale: The specification pairs infrared with electrical heaters and cooking food; the hot element emits infrared, which the surface of the food absorbs.

options.text: Ultraviolet, because the element glows white
options.rationale: A bright glow is taken as evidence of ultraviolet; the visible glow only shows the element is very hot.

options.text: Radio waves, because they carry heat energy
options.rationale: Any invisible radiation is labelled 'radio waves' by a student who does not separate the groups.

mcqs.stem: An infrared camera is used to find a person standing in a dark field at night. Why does the person show up on the image?

options.text: The camera shines visible light on the person
options.rationale: A camera is assumed to have to illuminate the scene; an infrared camera detects emitted radiation instead.

options.text: Infrared from the body can be seen by the eye too
options.rationale: The red glow of a heater is mistaken for infrared, so infrared is believed to be visible.

options.text: The person reflects ultraviolet from the night sky above
options.rationale: Ultraviolet is remembered as invisible and so is pressed into service for night vision; it is not what the camera detects.

options.text: Their body gives out infrared that the camera detects
options.rationale: The specification pairs infrared with infrared cameras; a warm body emits infrared, which the camera detects even in total darkness.

mcqs.stem: Which type of electromagnetic wave carries the signals in a fibre optic cable?

options.text: Visible light, sent as very rapid pulses
options.rationale: The specification pairs visible light with fibre optic communications; information travels as pulses of light along the glass fibre.

options.text: Microwaves, as used for satellite phone links
options.rationale: Any fast long-distance link is assumed to be a microwave link; the fibre carries light.

options.text: Radio waves, as used for television aerials
options.rationale: The cable is assumed to carry the same kind of signal as a television aerial receives.

options.text: Infrared, which warms the glass fibre
options.rationale: Infrared is linked only with heating, so the fibre is imagined to be warmed rather than carrying a signal.

mcqs.stem: A sunbed is used to give a tan. Which statement about the radiation it uses is correct?

options.text: It gives out infrared, and the heat browns skin
options.rationale: The warmth felt on a sunbed is taken as the cause of the tan; the tan is produced by ultraviolet.

options.text: It gives out visible light, which the skin absorbs
options.rationale: The visible glow of the tubes is assumed to be doing the tanning.

options.text: It gives out ultraviolet, which can harm skin
options.rationale: The specification pairs ultraviolet with sun tanning; ultraviolet darkens the skin but is absorbed by skin cells and can damage them.

options.text: Its ultraviolet is safe because the dose is small
options.rationale: A sunbed is seen as controlled and therefore harmless; the ultraviolet still risks damaging skin cells.

mcqs.stem: Why does a broken bone show up clearly on an X-ray photograph?

options.text: X-rays pass through bone but are absorbed by flesh
options.rationale: The pale and dark regions of the image are read the wrong way round, reversing the absorption.

options.text: X-rays are reflected from the surface of the bone
options.rationale: X-rays are treated like light striking a mirror, so the image is thought to be formed by reflection.

options.text: X-rays make the bone give out light of its own
options.rationale: The bright image is imagined to come from the bone itself rather than from a shadow.

options.text: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone
options.rationale: Bone absorbs X-rays far more strongly than flesh does, so a shadow of the bone, and of the break in it, falls on the detector.

mcqs.stem: Gamma rays are used in hospitals to treat cancer. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Gamma rays leave the treated tissue permanently radioactive
options.rationale: Irradiation is confused with contamination, so the patient is thought to become a source of radiation.

options.text: Gamma rays are far too dangerous ever to be used here
options.rationale: The hazard of gamma rays is remembered but the controlled medical use is not.

options.text: A beam of gamma rays is aimed at the tumour to kill cells
options.rationale: The specification pairs X-rays and gamma rays with medical treatments; a directed beam destroys the cells of the tumour.

options.text: Gamma rays are used only to photograph broken bones
options.rationale: Gamma rays are merged with X-ray imaging, so the treatment application is overlooked.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) Explain why microwaves rather than infrared are used to send signals to a communications satellite.

options.text: Microwaves travel much faster through space than infrared can
options.rationale: Waves of higher frequency are assumed to travel faster; all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum.

options.text: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere, infrared does not
options.rationale: The atmosphere transmits microwaves, so the signal reaches the satellite and returns; infrared is strongly absorbed by gases and water vapour in the air.

options.text: Infrared cannot cross the vacuum of space, but microwaves do
options.rationale: Infrared is tied to heating through a medium, so it is thought to need one; infrared from the Sun crosses space to reach us.

options.text: Microwaves are the only waves a dish aerial can send
options.rationale: The dish is assumed to work with one group of waves only; the choice is made by what the atmosphere transmits.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) An energy efficient lamp produces ultraviolet inside its tube, yet the room is lit by visible light. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: A coating absorbs ultraviolet and emits visible light
options.rationale: The fluorescent coating on the inside of the tube absorbs the ultraviolet and re-emits the energy as visible light, so the room is lit without ultraviolet leaving the lamp.

options.text: The lamp is designed to send ultraviolet into the room
options.rationale: The pairing of ultraviolet with these lamps is read as what the lamp emits; the ultraviolet is converted inside the tube.

options.text: The ultraviolet itself is the light you see the room by
options.rationale: Ultraviolet is treated as a kind of visible light because it comes from a lamp.

options.text: Ultraviolet reflects inside and is turned into heat energy
options.rationale: Any conversion of radiation is assumed to end as heating rather than as visible light.
